Designing Onboarding That Sticks

By a product designer · 8 min read · Share this on social media platforms today

Designing Onboarding That Sticks

Most onboarding flows are tours of features, and most users skip them within seconds. The flows that actually retain people do something different: they teach one habit and prove value before asking for anything.

1. Find the activation moment

Every product has a moment where a new user first feels the value, and onboarding exists to get people there quickly. For a note app it is finding an old note in seconds; for a design tool it is exporting a first screen that looks professional.

Measure how long new users take to reach that moment, because shortening that time is the single most reliable lever for activation.

2. Teach one habit, not ten features

Feature tours overload working memory, so people remember almost nothing from them. Instead, pick the one repeated action that predicts retention and design the first session around performing it twice.

Repetition in the first session matters more than coverage, since a habit needs a second rep before it starts to stick.

3. Use empty states as instructions

An empty screen is the most valuable real estate in onboarding because the user is already looking at it. Replace blank lists with one clear action and an example of what a filled state looks like.

4. Ask for permissions at the moment of need

Permission prompts shown on launch get denied because the user has no reason to say yes yet. Ask for notifications only after the user has done something worth being notified about, and explain the benefit in their words.

Onboarding is not a tutorial. It is the shortest path to the first moment of value.
